analysis.one_liner: Caps the U.S. price of taxpayer-funded drugs at the median price in comparable wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; after its initial referral it sat untouched until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires any company that develops a drug, vaccine, medical device, or diagnostic with federal research funding to agree to sell it in the U.S. at a reasonable price, capped at the median price in Canada and six other large, high-income countries. It also requires companies to report the cost of their clinical trials, federal subsidies, and revenues, with those reports made public. The Health and Human Services Secretary could waive the price cap, but only after public notice, comment, and a published economic justification.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs, vaccines, medical devices, and diagnostics that were developed at least partly with federal research money. Because Americans currently pay some of the highest drug prices in the world, tying the U.S. price to the median in comparable countries would directly lower out-of-pocket and insurance costs for those products. Taxpayers also benefit by getting a return on the research they fund rather than subsidizing discoveries that are then sold back to them at premium prices.

how_it_helps.text: Any federal agency funding biomedical research must require, as a condition of the funding or of a license to a patent or test data, that the resulting product be priced reasonably, as determined by HHS.
The reasonable price is capped at the median price charged in Canada and six other large, high-income OECD economies, so U.S. residents cannot be charged more than patients in comparable countries.
Manufacturers must report clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual revenues by country of sale, and HHS must make those reports publicly available.
HHS may adopt additional mechanisms, such as lowering prices when revenues exceed targets or when prices are barriers to access.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical, biotech, and medical device companies that commercialize products developed with federal funding would earn less U.S. revenue on those products. Supporters would respond that taxpayers already paid for the underlying research.

drawbacks.text: Industry and many researchers argue that capping prices on federally funded discoveries could reduce private investment in bringing early-stage science to market, since federal funding typically covers only the basic research phase while companies bear most of the clinical development cost and risk.
The bill applies only to products developed with federal funding or licensed federal patents and test data, leaving most drug prices untouched, so its scope is narrower than a general drug price cap.

The Secretary can waive the pricing obligation in the public interest, which could weaken the guarantee depending on how future administrations use that authority — though the waiver requires public comment and a published economic analysis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but asymmetric: patients and taxpayers stand to gain directly lower prices on products they partly funded, while manufacturers lose some U.S. revenue on a subset of their portfolios. The strongest objection — that price caps chill follow-on private investment — is a genuine risk but is blunted by the bill's narrow scope and its investor-incentive provisions, which let HHS tailor rules rather than impose a flat cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee, but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on August 10, 2021, joined by seven original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on August 11, 2021, to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug and device makers are better off, because the U.S. remains free to pay higher-than-peer-country prices on products developed with federal funding. Committee leadership never had to take a recorded position on the bill.

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over health legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and its Health subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support (the sponsor and 11 Democratic cosponsors), but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would cap the U.S. price of any drug or vaccine developed with federal research funding at the median price in peer countries, cutting U.S. revenue on those products. Its interest in blocking the bill runs against patients who would pay less.

The bill's pricing requirement covers devices, diagnostic tests, and other health technologies developed with federal funding, not just prescription drugs. Cheaper tests and devices would directly lower what patients and insurers pay.

Institutions that license federally funded patents would have to attach reasonable-pricing terms to those licenses, adding conditions to a revenue stream, though their research funding itself is unaffected.
